from: a first month in the accounts office
to: running a finance department and answering to auditors, banks and a foreign parent
case_setting: a named part of a finance department
series_arc: first month in the accounts office → **running a department and speaking for the company**
learners: They work, or are about to work, in the finance department of a Syrian company, factory, trading house or organisation — where English is the language of the group pack, of the auditors' working papers and of the paper trail: bank facility letters, letters of credit, supplier claims, donor reports, audit confirmations and the messages that arrive from a parent company abroad.
neutral: It is **desk-neutral within finance**. One cohort can contain a payables clerk, a payroll supervisor and a management accountant, and all three practise the same skill on their own part of the ledger.
contexts_intro: The programme assumes learners work on different parts of the ledger, not one. Twelve finance contexts carry the case studies:
contexts: Banks, letters of credit and transfers
Tax and the directorate of finance
Group reporting to a foreign parent
upward: **Upward and outward paper:** reconciliations and incident notes, monthly packs, variance explanations, decision papers for a director, claims on suppliers, submissions to a directorate of finance and replies to auditors — usually written, usually read by somebody who was not there.
contact: **Bank, auditor and parent-company contact:** a foreign parent's reporting office, group and local auditors, correspondent banks, overseas suppliers and donors, often where neither side is a native speaker.
reading_rows: Notes, slips, statements, messages, ledger pages — 138–190 words
Incident notes, variance explanations, options papers, claims — 208–288 words
Decision papers, standards, submissions, hearings — 290–358 words
writing_rows: Notes, slips, logs, a three-line handover — 45–71 words
Decision papers, standards, appraisals, submissions — 151–232 words
move3: Decide, supervise, and speak for the company
resp2: a ledger, a figure and a deadline
resp2b: a ledger, a figure and a deadline
arc2: someone who owns a ledger, a figure and a deadline
threads: **being honest about what you did not do and cannot evidence** (Course 1 S9 → Course 2 S14 → Course 3 S28); **giving a number its unit, basis and source** (C1 S4 → C2 S16 and S20 → C3 S27); and **writing so that the reader can act** (C1 S12 → C2 S19 → C3 S25).
h1: from your first day in the accounts office to a clerk the department can rely on
h2: from dependable pair of hands to owning a ledger, a figure and a deadline
h3: from owning a ledger to running a department and answering to auditors, banks and a foreign parent
map_example: A learner on the payroll desk meets their own work in sessions 10, 17 and 32, each time at a higher level of responsibility.
posts1: Accounts clerk · payables or receivables assistant · cashier · payroll assistant · stores and stock clerk · bank reconciliation clerk · audit trainee taking calls and messages
gives1: Being understood in the office and at a counter, taking a figure accurately, keeping a ledger and a register a second person can trust, answering for the department on the telephone, holding a control under pressure, accounting for a month and handing it on
posts2: Senior accounts clerk · payables or receivables supervisor · payroll supervisor · management accountant · cost accountant · treasury assistant · internal audit assistant
gives2: Owning a ledger and a figure: explaining an error so a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on a live ledger, explaining why a figure moved, pressing a claim on a supplier, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen
posts3: Chief accountant · financial controller · head of payables or receivables · internal audit manager · finance manager · deputy finance director
gives3: Other people's work and the company's word: delegating, appraising, chairing the month-end review, writing the standard a department follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with banks and suppliers, disagreeing upward, and answering a directorate of finance
constraint: a capable young accountant at the staff grade
sub1: From your first day in the accounts office to a clerk the department can rely on
sub2: From dependable pair of hands to owning a ledger, a figure and a deadline
sub3: From owning a ledger to running a department and answering to auditors, banks and a foreign parent
arc1_text: The learner arrives in a finance department unable to operate, and leaves able to be relied on: to take a figure accurately, keep a ledger and a register a second person can trust, answer for the department on the telephone, be trusted with cash, documents and a bank mandate, hold a control under pressure, account for a month and hand it on.
arc2_text: The learner is given something of their own — a ledger, a supplier account, a payroll, a figure — and learns the language that ownership requires: explaining an error so that a reader who was not there can follow it, training somebody on a live ledger, explaining why a figure moved, pressing a claim on a supplier, recommending with a reservation, and reporting upward including what did not happen.
arc3_text: The learner becomes answerable for other people's work and for the company's word. Three sessions are given to supervision itself — delegating, appraising and chairing — and the course runs on through writing the standard a department follows, naming risk before it lands, negotiating with banks and suppliers, answering a directorate of finance, and arguing for the learner's own next post.
